claim: SOX4 expression is increased in many human cancers.
source: The expression of the transcription factor SOX4 is increased in many human cancers, however, the pro-oncogenic capacity of SOX4 can vary greatly depending on the type of tumor.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about SOX4 expression patterns across cancer types.

claim: The pro-oncogenic capacity of SOX4 can vary greatly depending on the type of tumor.
source: The expression of the transcription factor SOX4 is increased in many human cancers, however, the pro-oncogenic capacity of SOX4 can vary greatly depending on the type of tumor.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general observation about SOX4 function.

claim: In mammary tumorigenesis, the SOX4 transcriptional network is dictated by the epigenome.
source: Here, we demonstrate that in mammary tumorigenesis, the SOX4 transcriptional network is dictated by the epigenome and is enriched for pro-angiogenic processes.
evidence: This claim is supported by ChIP-seq data showing SOX4 binding patterns correlate with active chromatin marks.

claim: The SOX4 transcriptional network is enriched for pro-angiogenic processes.
source: Here, we demonstrate that in mammary tumorigenesis, the SOX4 transcriptional network is dictated by the epigenome and is enriched for pro-angiogenic processes.
evidence: This is supported by GO-term analysis showing enrichment for blood vessel morphogenesis.

claim: SOX4 directly regulates endothelin-1 (ET-1) expression.
source: We show that SOX4 directly regulates endothelin-1 (ET-1) expression and can thereby promote tumor-induced angiogenesis both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq showing SOX4 binding to the EDN1 promoter, luciferase assays, and pull-down assays.

claim: SOX4 can promote tumor-induced angiogenesis both in vitro and in vivo.
source: We show that SOX4 directly regulates endothelin-1 (ET-1) expression and can thereby promote tumor-induced angiogenesis both in vitro and in vivo.
evidence: This is supported by in vitro assays (wound healing, sprouting, network formation) and in vivo zebrafish and mouse xenograft models.

claim: In breast tumors, SOX4 expression correlates with blood vessel density and size.
source: Furthermore, in breast tumors, SOX4 expression correlates with blood vessel density and size, and predicts poor-prognosis in patients with breast cancer.
evidence: This is supported by IHC analysis of patient tumor samples showing correlation between SOX4 and CD34 staining.

claim: SOX4 expression predicts poor-prognosis in patients with breast cancer.
source: Furthermore, in breast tumors, SOX4 expression correlates with blood vessel density and size, and predicts poor-prognosis in patients with breast cancer.
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis of patient cohorts.

claim: Sox4-deficient mice die during embryogenesis due to defective cardio-vasculature development.
source: Sox4-deficient mice die during embryogenesis due to defective cardio-vasculature development (Schilham et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: SOX4 controls the development of specific tissues, including lymphoid, pancreatic, brain and bone.
source: In addition, SOX4 controls the development of specific tissues, including lymphoid, pancreatic, brain and bone (Vervoort et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The expression of SOX4 in adult tissues is mostly restricted to adult stem- and progenitor cell populations including intestinal and hematopoietic stem cells.
source: In contrast to its wide-spread expression during embryogenesis, the expression of SOX4 in adult tissues is mostly restricted to adult stem- and progenitor cell populations including intestinal and hematopoietic stem cells (Sarkar and Hochedlinger, 2013; Vervoort et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SOX4 expression in human cancers has been positively correlated with tumor-progression in a wide-variety of solid and hematopoietic tumors.
source: SOX4 expression in human cancers has been positively correlated with tumor-progression in a wide-variety of solid and hematopoietic tumors (Lourenço and Coffer, 2017; Vervoort et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SOX4 hypomorphic mice have decreased cancer-incidence and a resistance to carcinogen-induced skin cancer.
source: Accordingly, SOX4 hypomorphic mice have decreased cancer-incidence and a resistance to carcinogen-induced skin cancer (Foronda et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: SOX4 endows tumor cells with a more migratory and invasive phenotype.
source: A recurring theme is that SOX4 endows tumor cells with a more migratory and invasive phenotype.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies showing this effect in various cancer types.

claim: SOX4 expression correlates with increased depth of invasion in clinical specimens.
source: Moreover, SOX4 expression correlates with increased depth of invasion in clinical specimens (Fang et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The overlap of transcriptional targets in different studies has proven to be very limited, suggesting that SOX4 has context-dependent effects on tumor development.
source: However, despite the similarity in phenotype that SOX4 confers in the various cell types, the overlap of transcriptional targets in the different studies has proven to be very limited (Vervoort et al., 2013a) suggesting that SOX4 has context-dependent effects on tumor development.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and inference from the literature.

claim: In breast cancer, SOX4 is directly controlled by miRNA-335, the loss of which is associated with disease progression and poor metastasis-free survival.
source: In breast cancer, SOX4 is directly controlled by miRNA-335, the loss of which is associated with disease progression and poor metastasis-free survival (Tavazoie et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: SOX4 has been demonstrated to be a part of gene signatures associated with metastasis of breast tumors to the brain and lungs.
source: SOX4 has also been demonstrated to be a part of gene signatures associated with metastasis of breast tumors to the brain and lungs (Minn et al., 2005; Bos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SOX4 has been shown to control the TGF-β-induced epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT).
source: Moreover, SOX4 has been shown to control the TGF-β-induced epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition (EMT), a process associated with increases in tumor-initiating cells, in invasive and migratory capacity, in metastasis and in drug resistance (Zhang et al., 2012; Tiwari et al., 2013; Kalluri, 2009; Vervoort et al., 2013b; Lourenço and Coffer, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SOX4-mediated induction of EMT has been proposed to be mediated by direct regulation of the histone-lysine N-methyltransferase EZH2.
source: In mice, SOX4-mediated induction of EMT has been proposed to be mediated by direct regulation of the histone-lysine N-methyltransferase EZH2, resulting in alterations in local histone three lysine (K) 27 trimethyl (H3K27me3) occupancy followed by changes in expression of EMT-associated genes (Tiwari et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Depletion of SOX4 has been shown to reduce metastasis formation in mouse models of breast cancer.
source: In line with its increased metastasis-associated expression and role in EMT, depletion of SOX4 has also been shown to reduce metastasis formation in mouse models of breast cancer (Tiwari et al., 2013; Tavazoie et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The context-dependent nature of the SOX4 transcriptional response can in part be explained by cell-type-specific expression of cooperating transcription factors.
source: The context-dependent nature of the SOX4 transcriptional response can in part be explained by cell-type-specific expression of cooperating transcription factors (Wilson and Koopman, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and general knowledge about transcription factor function.

claim: In murine pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA), the cell-type-specific expression of KLF5 can redirect the SOX4-mediated TGF-β transcriptional network from a pro-apoptotic to a pro-tumorigenic response.
source: Recently, it has been demonstrated in murine pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDA) that, the cell-type-specific expression of KLF5 can redirect the SOX4-mediated TGF-β transcriptional network from a pro-apoptotic to a pro-tumorigenic response, thus preventing lethal EMT (David et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: SOX4-bound loci were successfully identified in both HMLE wild-type (WT), untreated and DOX-treated HMLE-S4 cells.
source: SOX4-bound loci were successfully identified in both HMLE wild-type (WT), untreated and DOX-treated HMLE-S4 cells and, as expected, the largest number of peaks was uniquely bound in DOX-treated HMLE-S4 cells (Figure 1A), as reflected by an increased SOX4 occupancy on the HDAC2 promoter (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SOX4 binding was enriched at TSS-proximal sites, compared to random genomic regions.
source: In HMLE WT cells, untreated and DOX-treated HMLE-S4 cells, SOX4 binding was enriched at TSS-proximal sites, compared to random genomic regions (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–E), indicating that SOX4 binding is enriched at promoter regions.
evidence: This is supported by genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: SOX4 was identified as the most highly enriched motif in DOX-treated HMLE-S4 cells.
source: As expected, the SOX4-consensus DNA-binding motif was the most highly enriched motif in DOX-treated HMLE-S4 cells (Figure 1C) and was present in over 67% of all peaks.
evidence: This is supported by de novo motif analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The SOX4 consensus motif was centrally enriched in the identified peaks.
source: The SOX4 consensus motif was also centrally enriched in the identified peaks, further confirming sequence-dependent binding (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by motif density analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: SOX4-binding sites were centrally enriched in histone marks associated with active and open chromatin (H3K4me3 and H3K27ac), as well as in high levels of POL2.
source: SOX4-binding sites were centrally enriched in histone marks associated with active and open chromatin (H3K4me3 and H3K27ac), as well as in high levels of POL2, whereas the repressive mark H3K27me3 was absent from SOX4-bound sites (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq occupancy plots shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The repressive mark H3K27me3 was absent from SOX4-bound sites.
source: SOX4-binding sites were centrally enriched in histone marks associated with active and open chromatin (H3K4me3 and H3K27ac), as well as in high levels of POL2, whereas the repressive mark H3K27me3 was absent from SOX4-bound sites (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq occupancy plots shown in Figure 1E.

claim: SOX4-bound sites have significantly higher occupancy for H3K27ac, H3K4me3 and POL2 compared to unbound sites.
source: Quantitative analysis of SOX4-bound versus -unbound H3K27ac sites revealed that SOX4-bound sites have significantly higher occupancy for H3K27ac, H3K4me3 and POL2 compared to unbound sites, and are devoid of H3K27me3 occupancy (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: SOX4 preferentially binds to active/open chromatin.
source: These findings indicate that SOX4 preferentially binds to active/open chromatin.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing enrichment at active chromatin marks.

claim: Induction of SOX4 results in a concomitant increase in POL2 and H3K27ac occupancy.
source: This revealed that induction of SOX4 results in a concomitant increase in POL2 and H3K27ac occupancy (Figure 1G), which is also apparent at the genomic locus surrounding the validated SOX4 target gene TEAD2 (Figure 1H) (Bhattaram et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1G and genomic tracks in Figure 1H.

claim: Increased binding of SOX4 to regions of open chromatin promotes an active chromatin-state.
source: Taken together, these findings show that increased binding of SOX4 to regions of open chromatin promotes an active chromatin-state.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing increased active marks upon SOX4 binding.

claim: Analysis of overlap between SOX4-bound sites in HMLE cells and sites identified in two distinct breast cancer cell lines revealed a minor degree of overlap in SOX4-bound loci.
source: Indeed, analysis of overlap between SOX4-bound sites in HMLE cells and sites identified in two distinct breast cancer cell lines, the HER2-amplified HCC1954 cells and highly metastatic triple-negative MDA-MB-231 cells, revealed a minor degree of overlap in SOX4-bound loci, although the overlap on the associated genes was higher (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–I).
evidence: This is supported by Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H–I.

claim: SOX4 utilizes a pre-existing chromatin-landscape by binding to open/active chromatin.
source: SOX4 thus utilizes a pre-existing chromatin-landscape by binding to open/active chromatin, and binding to these sites subsequently increases the occupancy of active histone-marks and POL2.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing SOX4 binding patterns.

claim: 1378 genes were significantly regulated (q-value < 0.05) and differentially expressed by at least two-fold upon conditional SOX4 activation.
source: Data analysis revealed that 1378 genes were significantly regulated (q-value < 0.05) and differentially expressed by at least two-fold upon conditional SOX4 activation (Figure 2A), whereas no significantly altered genes were identified in ER HMLE control cells.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A core set of 650 genes were shown to be bound and transcriptionally regulated by SOX4.
source: This revealed a core set of 650 genes, which were shown to be bound and transcriptionally regulated by SOX4 (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: This is supported by overlap analysis of RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2B–C.

claim: The largest fraction of genes (63%) showed increased expression upon SOX4 activation.
source: Notably, the largest fraction of genes showed increased expression upon SOX4 activation (63%), while a considerably smaller percentage were found to be repressed targets (37%).
evidence: This is derived from analysis of the RNA-seq data.

claim: For all selected target genes, SOX4 conditional activation resulted in a time-dependent increase in expression.
source: For all selected target genes, SOX4 conditional activation resulted in a time-dependent increase in expression, with no significant change in the expression in ER-control HMLE cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR validation shown in Figure 2D.

claim: SOX4 predominantly acts as a transcriptional activator.
source: In support of the notion that SOX4 predominantly acts as a transcriptional activator, gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA), probing for enrichment of SOX4-bound genes (ChIP-seq, 2 kb from TSS) in the RNA-seq dataset demonstrated a significant and positive enrichment of SOX4-bound genes (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 2E and additional analyses in Figure 2F and supplementary figures.

claim: Only positively regulated SOX4 target genes were significantly enriched for SOX4 binding.
source: Furthermore, only positively regulated SOX4 target genes were significantly enriched for SOX4 binding as determined by hypergeometric testing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by hypergeometric testing shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: A significant increase in SOX4 occupancy upon DOX-treatment of HMLE-S4 cells was observed with peaks associated with the top 1000 induced genes.
source: Finally, a significant increase in SOX4 occupancy upon DOX-treatment of HMLE-S4 cells was observed with peaks associated with the top 1000 induced genes (Figure 2F), whereas no significant change was observed for peaks associated with repressed genes (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Inhibitory effects on gene expression are the result of indirect secondary mechanisms.
source: Taken together, these findings strongly indicate that SOX4 is a transcriptional activator and suggest that inhibitory effects on gene expression are the result of indirect secondary mechanisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq and ChIP-seq data showing SOX4 primarily activates genes.

claim: SOX4-target genes strongly correlated with decreased survival only in Claudinlow breast cancers.
source: In agreement with the observation that SOX4 transcriptional networks are context-dependent and directed in part by the epigenome, we observed that SOX4-target genes strongly correlated with decreased survival only in Claudinlow breast cancers (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Only a moderate correlation with survival was observed in Luminal and normal-like breast cancers.
source: In contrast, only a moderate correlation with survival was observed in Luminal and normal-like breast cancers and no significant correlation was observed in Basal-like breast cancers (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated based on analysis of patient data.

claim: SOX4 transcriptional networks may be breast cancer subtype specific.
source: These findings suggest that SOX4 transcriptional networks may be breast cancer subtype specific.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential survival correlations across breast cancer subtypes.

claim: GO-term analysis of SOX4 core genes showed a significant association with blood vessel morphogenesis.
source: GO-term analysis of SOX4 core genes showed a significant association with blood vessel morphogenesis, in addition to cell cycle- and cell migration-associated processes (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by GO-term analysis shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SOX4 target genes were enriched for genes encoding secreted proteins that are involved in cell migration, extra-cellular composition, angiogenesis and inflammation.
source: SOX4 target genes were also enriched for genes encoding secreted proteins that are involved in cell migration, extra-cellular composition, angiogenesis and inflammation (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B).
evidence: This is supported by GO-term analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–B.

claim: The association with vascular development and cell migration was restricted to the positively regulated gene-set.
source: The association with vascular development and cell migration was restricted to the positively regulated gene-set, whereas terms related to cell cycle and apoptosis were enriched in repressed genes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by GO-term analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C–D.

claim: EDN1 expression has been demonstrated to positively correlate with breast cancer tumor-grade and distant metastasis.
source: We chose to further evaluate the role of Endothelin-1 (EDN1) since its expression has been demonstrated to positively correlate with breast cancer tumor-grade and distant metastasis, and has been suggested to promote tumor-induced angiogenesis, migration and invasion (Salani et al., 2000; Wülfing et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: EDN1 has been suggested to promote tumor-induced angiogenesis, migration and invasion.
source: We chose to further evaluate the role of Endothelin-1 (EDN1) since its expression has been demonstrated to positively correlate with breast cancer tumor-grade and distant metastasis, and has been suggested to promote tumor-induced angiogenesis, migration and invasion (Salani et al., 2000; Wülfing et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Endothelin-1 (ET-1) directly induces angiogenesis by binding to its cognate receptors (ETAR and ETBR) expressed on endothelial cells.
source: Endothelin-1 (ET-1) directly induces angiogenesis by binding to its cognate receptors (ETAR and ETBR) expressed on endothelial cells (Rosanò et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Both EDN1 and its converting enzyme ECE-1 were observed to be transcriptionally induced.
source: Interestingly, both EDN1 and its converting enzyme ECE-1 were observed to be transcriptionally induced, indicating that SOX4 targets dual aspects of this pro-angiogenic pathway.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data.

claim: Analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq profiles of EDN1 locus indicated a strong increase in POL2 and H3K27ac upon DOX-mediated activation of SOX4 in HMLE-S4 cells.
source: In line with our previous observations, analysis of ChIP-seq and RNA-seq profiles of EDN1 locus indicated a strong increase in POL2 and H3K27ac upon DOX-mediated activation of SOX4 in HMLE-S4 cells (Figure 3C) and an increase in mRNA expression of EDN1 upon conditional activation of SOX4 in ERSOX4 HMLE cells (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq and RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: Induction of EDN1 expression was observed by qRT-PCR in ERSOX4 HMLE cells, and was absent in control ER HMLE cells.
source: This induction of EDN1 expression was also observed by qRT-PCR in ERSOX4 HMLE cells, and was absent in control ER HMLE cells (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: EDN1 was identified as a direct SOX4 target by ChIP in both MDA-MB-231 and HCC1954 cell lines.
source: EDN1 was also identified as a direct SOX4 target by ChIP in both MDA-MB-231 and HCC1954 cell lines (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H and data not shown).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP data.

claim: Upon shRNA-mediated knockdown of SOX4 in MDA-MB-231 and HCC1954 cell lines, EDN1 expression was decreased.
source: Indeed upon shRNA-mediated knockdown of SOX4 in these two cell lines we also observed that EDN1 expression was decreased (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B for MDA-MB-231 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2C for HCC1954).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: Two conserved SOX4 binding sites were identified at 70 bp and 350 bp from the TSS of the EDN1 promoter.
source: Closer examination of the EDN1 promoter overlapping SOX4 and H3K27ac profiles identified two conserved SOX4 binding sites at 70 bp and 350 bp from the TSS (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by ChIP-seq data and conservation analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Ectopic expression of SOX4 strongly induced luciferase expression as compared to the empty vector (EV) control.
source: Ectopic expression of SOX4 strongly induced luciferase expression as compared to the empty vector (EV) control, which could be inhibited by the co-transfection of a dominant negative truncated SOX4 lacking the transactivation domain (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: Activation of the luciferase reporter was significantly inhibited when the SOX4 binding site at −350 bp was mutated.
source: Activation of the luciferase reporter was significantly inhibited when the SOX4 binding site at −350 bp was mutated, whereas no significant reduction was observed upon mutation of the −70 bp site, indicating that transcriptional activation of EDN1 by SOX4 under these conditions is mediated by the site at −350 bp from the TSS (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: SOX4 was found to specifically bind to the conserved motifs at −350 bp from the EDN1 TSS.
source: SOX4 was found to specifically bind to the conserved motifs at −350 bp from the EDN1 TSS, which could be inhibited by mutation of this site (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by pull-down assay data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Conditional activation of SOX4 in HMLE resulted in a significant increase in ET-1 secretion by these cells.
source: Conditional activation of SOX4 in HMLE resulted in a significant increase in ET-1 secretion by these cells (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Exposure of HMEC-1 cells to SCM+ was capable of increasing migration of HMEC-1 cells.
source: Relative to basal media alone, exposure of HMEC-1 cells to SCM+ was capable of increasing migration of HMEC-1 cells, whereas no significant increase was observed with SCM- or ER-control HMLE conditioned media (ERCM+) (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by wound-healing assay data shown in Figure 4.

claim: SCM+-induced migration could be inhibited by the dual endothelin receptor antagonist Bosentan.
source: Importantly, SCM+-induced migration could be inhibited by the dual endothelin receptor antagonist Bosentan (Clozel et al., 1994), demonstrating that the pro-migratory effect indeed required endothelin receptor activation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by wound-healing assay data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: SCM+ did not affect HMEC-1 cell proliferation.
source: SCM+ did not affect HMEC-1 cell proliferation, indicating that wound-closure is exclusively dependent on cell migration (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Treatment of HMEC-1 cells with a synthetic ET-1 peptide resulted in a significant increase in wound closure.
source: Similar to SCM+, treatment of HMEC-1 cells with a synthetic ET-1 peptide resulted in a significant increase in wound closure, although not to the same extent as complete media which contains additional pro-migratory and pro-angiogenic factors (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by wound-healing assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: siRNA-mediated knockdown of EDN1 reduced the SCM+-induced migration in HMEC-1 cells.
source: In order to assess whether the SCM+-mediated effects required transcriptional induction of EDN1 by SOX4, siRNA-mediated knockdown of EDN1 was performed in HMLE cells 24 hr prior to conditional SOX4 activation. EDN1 knockdown reduced the SCM+-induced migration in HMEC-1 cells (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by wound-healing assay data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Stable expression of SOX4 in MDA-MB-231 cells resulted in increased EDN1 expression.
source: Similar to conditional activation in HMLE cells, stable expression of SOX4 in MDA-MB-231 cells also resulted in increased EDN1 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and conditioned media with the capacity to increase HMEC-1 migration (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR and wound-healing assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Figure 4E.

claim: SCM+ treatment of HMEC-1 cells resulted in an increase in the relative network length.
source: Relative to basal media alone, SCM+ treatment of HMEC-1 cells resulted in an increase in the relative network length, which could be inhibited by Bosentan, whereas no increase in network formation was observed in control conditions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by matrigel angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–E.

claim: Incubation with the ET-1 peptide significantly increased the network length.
source: Similarly, incubation with the ET-1 peptide significantly increased the network length, an effect that could also be inhibited by treatment with Bosentan (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by matrigel angiogenesis assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Both ET-1 and SCM+ treatment of HMEC-1 cells resulted in a marked increase in sprouting.
source: In this assay both ET-1 and SCM+ treatment of HMEC-1 cells resulted in a marked increase in sprouting, although less pronounced than full medium (Figure 4F–J).
evidence: This is supported by sprouting assay data shown in Figure 4F–J.

claim: SCM+ potently induced sprouting by approximately 6-fold which could be inhibited by Bosentan.
source: Relative to basal media, SCM+ potently induced sprouting in this assay by approximately 6-fold which could be inhibited by Bosentan (Figure 4F–G).
evidence: This is supported by sprouting assay data shown in Figure 4F–G.

claim: ET-1 induced sprouting by approximately 5-fold, which could also be completely inhibited by Bosentan.
source: Correspondingly, ET-1 induced sprouting by approximately 5-fold, which could also be completely inhibited by Bosentan (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by sprouting assay data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: siRNA mediated depletion of EDN1 prior to conditional SOX4 activation resulted in an almost complete inhibition of SCM+-induced sprouting.
source: Similar to the results obtained in the wound-closure assays, siRNA mediated depletion of EDN1 prior to conditional SOX4 activation resulted in an almost complete inhibition of SCM+-induced sprouting (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by sprouting assay data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: Conditioned media from SOX4 expressing MDA-MB-231 cells resulted in increased HMEC-1 sprouting.
source: Additionally, conditioned media from SOX4 expressing MDA-MB-231 cells also resulted in increased HMEC-1 sprouting (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by sprouting assay data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: shRNA-mediated knockdown of SOX4 in MDA-MB-231 cells resulted in a decrease of EDN1 expression.
source: In accordance, shRNA-mediated knockdown of SOX4 in MDA-MB-231 cells resulted in a decrease of EDN1 expression (Figure 6A–B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–B) and a concomitant decrease in the ability to induce migration and sprouting of endothelial cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–H).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR and functional assay data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: A significant increase in sprouting from the SIV was observed in 4-OHT treated ERSOX4 HMLE cells compared to untreated ERSOX4 HMLE cells.
source: A significant increase in sprouting from the SIV was observed in 4-OHT treated ERSOX4 HMLE cells compared to untreated ERSOX4 HMLE cells as well as both treated and untreated ER-control HMLE cells, indicating that conditional activation of SOX4 in HMLE cells can induce angiogenesis in vivo (Figure 5B–D).
evidence: This is supported by zebrafish xenograft data shown in Figure 5B–D.

claim: SOX4-depleted MDA-MB-231 cells were significantly impaired in their ability to induce ectopic sprouting from the SIV.
source: Quantification of neovascularization demonstrated that SOX4-depleted MDA-MB-231 cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) were significantly impaired in their ability to induce ectopic sprouting from the SIV, as illustrated by a decrease in the number of sprouting vessels and an overall reduction in the percentage of fish with sprouting blood vessels (Figure 5E–G).
evidence: This is supported by zebrafish xenograft data shown in Figure 5E–G.

claim: Depletion of ET-1 in SOX4-activated cells results in the reduction of angiogenic potential.
source: Similar to our previous observations in vitro, depletion of ET-1 in SOX4-activated cells results in the reduction of angiogenic potential, shown by the decreased capacity to induce ectopic sprouting from the SIV (Figure 5H–J).
evidence: This is supported by zebrafish xenograft data shown in Figure 5H–J.

claim: SOX4 controls tumor-induced angiogenesis in vivo, in an ET-1 dependent manner.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that, similar to our in vitro observations, SOX4 controls tumor-induced angiogenesis in vivo, in an ET-1 dependent manner.
evidence: This is inferred from the zebrafish xenograft experiments.

claim: Primary tumor growth was unaffected by SOX4 depletion.
source: Prior to injection, we validated the efficiency of SOX4 knockdown by qRT-PCR. This revealed a significant reduction in SOX4 expression in SOX4 KD MDA-MB-231 cells compared to scrambled control cells, which was accompanied by a significant decrease in EDN1 expression (Figure 6A–B). Following validation, cells were transplanted into the mammary fat-pad and we subsequently monitored tumor growth up to six weeks post-implantation. Primary tumor growth was unaffected by SOX4 depletion and both scrambled control and SOX4 KD mice were sacrificed in the same week (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth curve data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: SOX4 KD knockdown was maintained in vivo.
source: Analysis of primary tumors by immunohistochemistry (IHC) for SOX4, ET-1 and CD31 (PECAM-1) expression showed that SOX4 KD knockdown was maintained in vivo (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Quantitative analysis of ET-1 expression revealed a significant reduction in ET-1 IHC staining in SOX4 KD compared to scrambled control tumors.
source: Moreover, quantitative analysis of ET-1 expression revealed a significant reduction in ET-1 IHC staining in SOX4 KD compared to scrambled control tumors (Figure 6D–E).
evidence: This is supported by IHC quantification shown in Figure 6D–E.

claim: SOX4 KD tumors had significantly lower vascularization as illustrated by the reduction in total blood vessel area, blood vessel count and blood vessel size.
source: We next assessed tumor vascularization by quantifying expression of the endothelial cell surface marker CD31. SOX4 KD tumors had significantly lower vascularization as illustrated by the reduction in total blood vessel area, blood vessel count and blood vessel size (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by CD31 quantification shown in Figure 6F.

claim: SOX4 expression is required for tumor-associated ET-1 expression in vivo.
source: These findings demonstrate that SOX4 expression is required for tumor-associated ET-1 expression in vivo, and SOX4-depletion correlates with reduced tumor blood vessel density.
evidence: This is inferred from the xenograft mouse model data.

claim: SOX4-depletion correlates with reduced tumor blood vessel density.
source: These findings demonstrate that SOX4 expression is required for tumor-associated ET-1 expression in vivo, and SOX4-depletion correlates with reduced tumor blood vessel density.
evidence: This is supported by CD31 quantification in xenograft tumors.

claim: SOX4 depletion significantly reduced the development of lung metastases.
source: Importantly, SOX4 depletion in this orthotopic xenograft model also significantly reduced the development of lung metastases (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by metastasis quantification shown in Figure 6G.

claim: SOX4 can control multiple aspects of breast tumor biology.
source: Together, these findings demonstrate that SOX4 can control multiple aspects of breast tumor biology, and show for the first time that SOX4 may regulate tumor angiogenesis in vivo.
evidence: This is inferred from the xenograft mouse model data showing effects on angiogenesis and metastasis.

claim: Nuclear SOX4 expression was found to significantly correlate with tumor size, histological grade and mitotic index.
source: Nuclear SOX4 expression was found to significantly correlate with tumor size, histological grade and mitotic index, all parameters of poor-prognosis (Figure 7—source data 1, Figure 7—source data 2, Figure 7—source data 3, Figure 7—source data 4, Figure 7—source data 5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of patient TMA data.

claim: High levels of SOX4 expression significantly correlated with decreased overall survival in breast cancer patients.
source: Accordingly, high levels of SOX4 expression significantly correlated with decreased overall survival in breast cancer patients, and this was also observed when patients were subdivided into the major subtypes ILC and IDC (Figure 7C–E).
evidence: This is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 7C–E.

claim: Patients with high levels of SOX4 have a significantly worse prognosis in the ER-positive tumor group.
source: Stratification of patients with breast cancer according to the ER-status revealed that patients with high levels of SOX4 have a significantly worse prognosis in the ER-positive tumor group, and a trend towards poor-prognosis in the ER-negative tumor group (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The percentage of tumors with high SOX4 expression was observed to be significantly higher in those patients who develop metastasis as compared to patients who do not present with metastatic disease.
source: This revealed that the percentage of tumors with high SOX4 expression was observed to be significantly higher in those patients who develop metastasis as compared to patients who do not present with metastatic disease (p=0.016; Figure 7—source data 5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of patient data.

claim: SOX4 expression in the primary tumor reflects the expression level observed in the metastasis.
source: Moreover, analysis of SOX4 expression in 23 matched primary-tumor metastasis patient samples revealed that SOX4 expression in the primary tumor reflects the expression level observed in the metastasis (p=0.039; Figure 7—source data 5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of matched patient samples.

claim: SOX4 expression is a clear marker of poor-prognosis in breast cancer.
source: These observations indicate that SOX4 expression is a clear marker of poor-prognosis in breast cancer and underscore the important role of SOX4 in tumor-progression and metastasis observed in breast cancer model systems.
evidence: This is inferred from the patient survival and metastasis data.

claim: No significant benefit to patient survival was observed for adjuvant radio- or chemotherapy-treated SOX4-high tumors as compared to untreated tumors.
source: Interestingly, no significant benefit to patient survival was observed for adjuvant radio- or chemotherapy-treated SOX4-high tumors as compared to untreated tumors, whereas a significant treatment response was observed for SOX4-low tumors (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis stratified by treatment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: SOX4 may contribute to therapy resistance.
source: These findings suggest that SOX4 may also contribute to therapy resistance.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of treatment benefit in SOX4-high tumors.

claim: Tumors expressing high levels of SOX4 had a significantly increased total blood vessel area and size.
source: Quantitative analysis of CD34-staining revealed that tumors expressing high levels of SOX4 had a significantly increased total blood vessel area and size, with an apparent but non-significant increase in the total number of blood vessels, thus suggesting that SOX4 can influence tumor-induced angiogenesis in human breast cancer (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by CD34 quantification in patient tumors shown in Figure 7G.

claim: SOX4 can influence tumor-induced angiogenesis in human breast cancer.
source: Quantitative analysis of CD34-staining revealed that tumors expressing high levels of SOX4 had a significantly increased total blood vessel area and size, with an apparent but non-significant increase in the total number of blood vessels, thus suggesting that SOX4 can influence tumor-induced angiogenesis in human breast cancer (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is inferred from the correlation between SOX4 and blood vessel markers in patient tumors.

claim: SOX4 acts as an opportunistic transcription factor directed by a pre-existing chromatin landscape.
source: Our findings indicate that SOX4 acts as an opportunistic transcription factor directed by a pre-existing chromatin landscape, which upon recruitment to open chromatin further enhances the active chromatin-state.
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq data showing SOX4 binding patterns.

claim: Both the specific cell-type epigenome and the expression of co-factors are important in shaping the SOX4 transcriptional network.
source: These observations indicate that both the specific cell-type epigenome and the expression of co-factors are important in shaping the SOX4 transcriptional network, providing an explanation for the relatively minor degree of overlap in SOX4 target genes between cancer-types (Vervoort et al., 2013a).
evidence: This is inferred from the ChIP-seq and motif analysis data.

claim: The SOX4 core-signature is strongly predictive for survival specifically in the Claudinlow breast cancer subtype.
source: An important finding is that the SOX4 core-signature is strongly predictive for survival specifically in the Claudinlow breast cancer subtype.
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis in METABRIC cohort.

claim: Claudinlow breast tumors are characterized by cells that have undergone EMT, have extensive immune cell infiltration and also exhibit activation of the vasculature.
source: Previous studies have identified distinct clusters of genes that distinguish Claudinlow breast cancers from other subtypes. The nature of these gene clusters suggest that Claudinlow breast tumors are characterized by cells that have undergone EMT, have extensive immune cell infiltration and also exhibit activation of the vasculature (Prat and Perou, 2011; Taube et al., 2010; Harrell et al., 2014; Hennessy et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: EMT and TGF-β associated genes are significantly enriched in the SOX4 target gene dataset.
source: Accordingly, we find that EMT and TGF-β associated genes are significantly enriched in our SOX4 target gene dataset (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B), although major EMT associated transcription factors SNAI1, SNAI2 or TWIST1 were not observed to be regulated (data not shown) (Vervoort et al., 2013a; Tiwari et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B.

claim: The direct transcriptional network of SOX4 is not dependent on the induction of EZH2 in HMLE cells.
source: Despite a previous report that SOX4-mediated induction of EMT occurs through upregulation of EZH2 levels, we did not detect significant regulation of EZH2 upon conditional SOX4 activation in HMLE cells (data not shown). This suggests that the direct transcriptional network of SOX4 is not dependent on the induction of EZH2 in these cells.
evidence: This is based on RNA-seq data not showing EZH2 regulation.

claim: SOX4 may contribute to EMT and the TGF-β response in breast cancer on multiple levels.
source: These findings indicate that SOX4 may contribute to EMT and the TGF-β response in breast cancer on multiple levels.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of EMT and TGF-β genes in the SOX4 target dataset.

claim: SOX4-induced tumor angiogenesis may contribute to metastatic dissemination.
source: SOX4-induced tumor angiogenesis may also contribute to metastatic dissemination.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed effects on angiogenesis and metastasis.

claim: Depletion of SOX4 leads to a reduced number of spontaneous lung metastases in a xenograft model.
source: We have shown that depletion of SOX4 leads to a reduced number of spontaneous lung metastases in a xenograft model, which correlated with decreased ET-1 expression and blood vessel density.
evidence: This is supported by xenograft mouse model data.

claim: Gene signatures associated with vascular activation in Claudinlow tumors were predictive for metastatic dissemination.
source: It has been previously reported that gene signatures associated with vascular activation in Claudinlow tumors were predictive for metastatic dissemination(Harrell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: SOX4-regulated RNAseq data in HMLEs showed enrichment for vascular signatures.
source: Our SOX4-regulated RNAseq data in HMLEs showed enrichment for one of these vascular signatures (Figure 7—figure supplement 2C) suggesting that SOX4 may drive tumor angiogenesis in Claudinlow tumors by regulating these genes in addition to EDN1.
evidence: This is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2C.

claim: ET-1 expression has been demonstrated to positively correlate with tumor-grade and the formation of distant metastasis in breast cancer.
source: In agreement with a role in tumor-progression, ET-1 expression has been demonstrated to positively correlate with tumor-grade and the formation of distant metastasis in breast cancer (Wülfing et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: SOX4 induced ET-1 may promote tumor-progression in an autocrine manner by inducing EMT or affecting T-cell infiltration.
source: In addition to promoting angiogenesis, SOX4 induced ET-1 may also promote tumor-progression in an autocrine manner by inducing EMT or for example by affecting T-cell infiltration, both of which have demonstrated in ovarian cancer (Buckanovich et al., 2008; Rosanò et al., 2005; Rosanò et al., 2013).
evidence: This is speculated based on citations to previous work in other cancer types.

claim: Anti-angiogenic therapies targeting the VEGF-receptor pathway have been tested in clinical trials with limited success due to unwanted side-effects.
source: In the last decade a number of anti-angiogenic therapies, mostly targeting the VEGF-receptor pathway, have been tested in clinical trials with limited success due to unwanted side-effects (Jain, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: SOX4 is an interesting therapeutic target in breast cancer, allowing for the simultaneous inhibition of multiple biological processes required for tumor metastasis.
source: As a driver of both EMT and tumor-induced angiogenesis, SOX4 is an interesting therapeutic target in breast cancer, allowing for the simultaneous inhibition of multiple biological processes required for tumor metastasis.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed functions of SOX4.

claim: ETAR and ETBR receptor inhibitors such as Bosentan are currently used to treat pulmonary vascular hypertension.
source: Alternatively, ETAR and ETBR receptor inhibitors such as Bosentan are currently used to treat pulmonary vascular hypertension, and based on our results could potentially be repurposed to specifically treat aggressive SOX4HI breast tumors (Rosanò et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and speculation based on current findings.

claim: Promising results were obtained in a number of ovarian cancer patients when ET-1 receptor antagonists were combined with standard chemotherapeutics.
source: Although success of ET-1 receptor antagonists in the treatment of advanced cancers, including glioma and melanoma, has been limited, promising results were obtained in a number of ovarian cancer patients when combined with standard chemotherapeutics (Rosanò et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Patients with SOX4HI tumors are more likely to profit from treatment with ET-1 receptor antagonists.
source: Based on our findings, patients with SOX4HI tumors are more likely to profit from treatment with ET-1 receptor antagonists, thus arguing for the specific monitoring of this subgroup in future clinical studies.
evidence: This is speculated based on the findings showing SOX4 regulates ET-1.
